summary: Describes using entropy labels to improve load balancing across MPLS networks. It defines the concept, explains why such labels are useful, and lists properties that allow maximal benefit. It is a standards-track specification.

eli5.summary: If trucks all look alike, a road cannot split them evenly. An entropy label is like a random sticker so routers can spread the trucks across many roads.

subtitle: A spare label that lets MPLS routers balance traffic across paths without peeking inside packets.

tldr.problem: Transit routers in an MPLS network must spread packets over equal-cost paths while keeping each flow on one path. They often cannot tell what is inside an MPLS packet, so they hash only the labels and balance poorly.
tldr.mechanism: The ingress router, which knows the payload, hashes the flow's fields and pushes the result as an extra entropy label, preceded by a reserved Entropy Label Indicator (value 7). Transit routers can balance on the label stack alone, and egress routers signal that they can handle it.
tldr.outcome: The cost is two extra labels in the stack. The RFC updates RFC 3031, RFC 3107, RFC 3209 and RFC 5036, and is itself updated by later RFCs.

today: RFC 6790 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted, but it has been updated by RFC 7274, RFC 7447 and RFC 8012. It itself updates RFC 3031, RFC 3107, RFC 3209 and RFC 5036.

sections.title: Why MPLS Needs Entropy Labels
sections.content:
Load balancing spreads traffic over several paths. It eases capacity planning, absorbs traffic surges and gives resilience if a link or node fails. Two common techniques are Link Aggregation Group (LAG), which bonds several circuits between adjacent nodes, and Equal Cost Multi-Path (ECMP), which uses several shortest paths between nodes separated by one or more hops.

All packets of a flow must follow the same path, to avoid jitter, latency and reordering. A node therefore feeds chosen header fields (keys) into a hash function. For IP, typical keys are the source and destination addresses, the protocol type and the TCP or UDP ports. In MPLS, a transit Label Switching Router (LSR) may have to look deep into the packet to find them, and often cannot tell what the payload is. It then hashes the top label or all labels, which are coarse and can give very uneven distribution.

The idea in RFC 6790 is to let the ingress LSR do the work. It extracts the keys, hashes them and puts the result in an additional entropy label in the stack. Transit LSRs can then balance on the label stack alone.
sections.eli5: It is easier for the first post office, which can see what is in each parcel, to write a code on the outside than for every later post office to open the parcels.

sections.title: Design Choices
sections.content:
The RFC compares two ways to carry load-balancing information. One allocates several equivalent labels per Forwarding Equivalence Class (FEC); the stack depth stays the same, but signaling and forwarding state grow significantly. The other adds one label to the stack, with minimal change to signaling state and none to transit forwarding. The RFC takes the second approach.

Because the entropy label is generated by the ingress and the application label is allocated downstream, the two could be confused. The RFC chooses a reserved Entropy Label Indicator (ELI) placed just before the entropy label. The alternatives, a pair of labels per FEC or allowing entropy labels only where no confusion is possible, doubled state or were too restrictive.

Entropy labels are tied to tunnels (LSPs) rather than to applications such as VPNs. The RFC gives four reasons: there are few tunneling protocols but many applications, so the standards stay simpler; there is less churn as new services appear; tunnel labels are simpler to process than application labels; and each layer of a hierarchy such as LDP over RSVP-TE can choose independently. The net cost is two labels: the ELI and the entropy label.
sections.eli5: They could give each parcel route many different tickets, which needs lots of paperwork, or just add one extra sticker. They chose the sticker, plus a small flag saying "the next sticker is the random one."

sections.title: What an Entropy Label Is
sections.content:
An entropy label (EL) is a label that is not used for forwarding, is not signaled, and exists only to add entropy for load balancing. It is generated by the ingress LSR purely from load-balancing information. Its value must not be in the reserved label space (0-15).

The egress LSR must be able to tell an entropy label from an application label. So the label immediately before an entropy label, closer to the top of the stack, is required to be the ELI. The ELI is a reserved label with value 7.

The RFC notes that entropy labels are also useful for pseudowires. RFC 6391 covers pseudowires of the RFC 4447 style, and this memo covers tunnels and so all other MPLS applications.
sections.eli5: The entropy label is just a number that means nothing for steering. It is there to make traffic look different, and the flag label before it says "ignore the next one when steering."

sections.title: Handling Entropy Labels in the Data Plane
sections.content:
Ingress. An ingress LSR X may insert an entropy label only if the egress Y has signaled that it can process them for that tunnel, and X must not otherwise. X identifies the application, hashes the chosen fields, pushes the application label if any, picks the tunnel label TL, and pushes <TL, ELI, EL>. The ELI should use the same TTL and TC as TL, and its BoS bit must be zero. The EL's TTL must be zero so it is never used for forwarding. X may insert several ELI and EL pairs, one per hierarchical tunnel, where the egress of each allows it.

Transit. Transit LSRs may operate with no change. One that recognizes the ELI may balance solely on the label after it; otherwise it should use as much of the label stack as feasible. Reserved labels must never be used as hash keys. Transit LSRs may still look beyond the stack when no ELI is present.

Egress. Y must handle packets with and without an EL. It pops the tunnel label, then the ELI and the EL, and the EL's TTL must be ignored. If any ELI it processes has the BoS bit set, Y must discard the packet. A penultimate-hop LSR needs no change, but may pop the ELI and EL along with the tunnel label if that does not hurt its ability to balance on the next hop.
sections.eli5: The first router adds the sticker and its flag. Middle routers can just read the sticker. The last router peels both off before delivering.

sections.title: Signaling Entropy Label Capability
sections.content:
An egress signals its Entropy Label Capability (ELC) per tunnel. Even if it signals implicit null, meaning penultimate hop popping is used, it must be prepared to pop the ELI and EL. The capability may be asymmetric between the two ends of a tunnel.

  • LDP: a new ELC TLV of Type 0x0206 and Length 0, carried as an optional parameter of the Label Mapping message. The U and F bits must both be 1. An LSR that does not understand it must pass it on intact. An LSR that understands it advertises ELC for a FEC only if every mapping it received for that FEC carried the TLV.
  • BGP: an optional, transitive path attribute of value 28, included only if the speaker sets NEXT_HOP to itself and can process entropy labels. It can be re-advertised unchanged where NEXT_HOP is unchanged (for example route reflectors) or labels are only swapped, and otherwise must be removed unless the re-advertiser meets the same two conditions.
  • RSVP-TE: the ELC flag, bit number 9, in the Attribute Flags TLV of the LSP_ATTRIBUTES object. In a Path message it means the ingress can process entropy labels upstream, which only makes sense for a bidirectional LSP. In a Resv message it means the egress can process them downstream.

Multicast LSPs seldom use ECMP, but can cross bundled links and LAGs, so entropy labels can help there. The RFC leaves the signaling and processing details to a future document.
sections.eli5: Before the first router uses the sticker trick, the last router has to say "I know how to peel those off." Each kind of messenger protocol has its own way to carry that note.

sections.title: OAM, MPLS-TP and Multicast
sections.content:
The RFC also affects testing tools. LSP traceroute (RFC 4379) asks transit LSRs for a range of label values that steer a packet along each path, but does not say where in the stack to put the value or whether deep packet inspection is allowed. This memo updates it: the value from the label range goes in the entropy label. An LSR may still use deep inspection, provided it does so consistently for both the range computation and the data path. For BFD sessions on a given path, a value from that path's label range should be used as the EL value of the BFD packets.

The MPLS Transport Profile (MPLS-TP) does not use ECMP, so entropy labels do not apply to an MPLS-TP deployment.
sections.eli5: When engineers test each road, they now put their test number in the sticker, so the test packets really take the road they want to check.

sections.title: Worked LDP Examples
sections.content:
Section 8 of the RFC is illustrative and not normative. It walks through LDP tunnels from ingress X through transit routers to egress Y. With ultimate hop popping and entropy labels, the stack <TL, ELI, EL> is swapped hop by hop and Y pops all three. With penultimate hop popping, the last transit router pops the tunnel label and Y receives <ELI, EL>. It also shows cases where Y signals capability but X chooses not to insert an EL.

With a VPN application label AL, the ingress sends <TL, ELI, EL, AL>. In an LDP over RSVP-TE case, the ELs are inserted for the LDP tunnel only and the RSVP-TE tunnel has none. The RFC adds that an ingress remembers per tunnel whether the egress can process entropy labels, but need not keep per-application state. It can decide per application: for example, skip them for circuit emulation but use them for an IP VPN over the same tunnel.
sections.eli5: The examples are like diagrams of a parcel traveling through several post offices, showing exactly which stickers are on it at each step and who removes them.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says it introduces no new security vulnerabilities to LDP, BGP or RSVP-TE, and refers to the security sections of RFC 5036, RFC 4271 and RFC 3209. End users have no control over entropy label values, so there is little risk of forgery that would unbalance the network.

If the EL is computed only from packet headers, an efficient wiretapping interface could be built depending on the hash function. An implementation can guard against this by adding another input, such as a random value, to the EL generation. If the capability is not signaled, for example through malicious configuration of the egress PE, the ingress simply falls back to not using entropy labels, which is no worse than current behavior. Operators are advised to monitor PE configuration changes and the fairness of load distribution.
sections.eli5: Nobody outside can pick the stickers, so they cannot easily cause trouble. If the last router refuses to take part, everyone just goes back to the old, less even way.
